questions.question: Q: Explain the link between obesity and type 2 diabetes.

points.text: Excess body fat, particularly visceral fat, causes cells to become resistant to insulin. The pancreas produces more insulin to compensate, but eventually cannot keep up, leading to elevated blood glucose levels (type 2 diabetes). Weight loss of 5-10% can significantly improve insulin sensitivity and in some cases reverse early type 2 diabetes.

points.text: The Soft Drinks Industry Levy led to a 29% reduction in sugar in soft drinks as manufacturers reformulated to avoid the tax. This reduces calorie and sugar intake, potentially reducing obesity and tooth decay. markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the UK's second leading cause of death, and diet plays a significant role in both increasing and reducing risk. The primary dietary risk factor is excessive saturated fat intake, which raises LDL ('bad') cholesterol. LDL cholesterol deposits in artery walls, forming plaques that narrow arteries (atherosclerosis), potentially leading to heart attacks and strokes. Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats (olive oil, oily fish) can lower LDL and raise HDL ('good') cholesterol, reducing CVD risk. Excess salt intake (UK average 8.4g/day vs recommended 6g/day) raises blood pressure, another major CVD risk factor. Processed foods contribute approximately 75% of dietary salt. Reducing salt intake by 1.6g/day could prevent approximately 5,000 deaths annually in the UK. Insufficient fruit and vegetable consumption means fewer protective antioxidants and less potassium (which helps lower blood pressure). The UK 5-a-day target is met by only about 30% of adults. Oily fish provides omega-3 fatty acids that reduce inflammation, lower triglycerides, and reduce blood clotting tendency. The recommended two portions per week (including one oily) is rarely met. However, diet alone cannot prevent CVD — physical inactivity, smoking, and genetic factors also contribute significantly. A comprehensive prevention strategy must address all modifiable risk factors.
